source_title: Premium: The Hater's Guide To Megaspeed
other_side: Zitron, in a paid piece published the day after of which only the opening is free to read, says the press is treating Huang's fall as tabloid material and missing the larger matter: his allegation that Nvidia misled people about how and where it makes its money. He repeats a short seller's claim that more than a fifth of last fiscal year's revenue may have come through diverted sales to China, and points to two earlier SEC actions against Nvidia over its disclosures. Where Whittemore mourns a load-bearing figure, Zitron concludes "we can't trust a damn word" Huang or Nvidia says. These are his allegations.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether Huang was holding the AI industry up or propping it up. Both accept as fact that he is out, that Nvidia's general counsel reportedly intervened in a Commerce Department probe, and that Nvidia's guarantees and investments underpin labs and neoclouds. The empirical question is whether that support, and Nvidia's reported revenue, survive scrutiny under new management; the observable is Nvidia's next results and guidance under its interim chief executive, and whether it keeps backstopping customers. The residue is worldview: whether one man's judgement built an industry or disguised its weakness. For Whittemore to be vindicated, Nvidia must stabilise while the losses fall on China ties, open models and the pace of building. For Zitron, investigators must show material diverted revenue and the financing web must contract. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both think Nvidia's backstops are the thing most at risk. Watch Nvidia's results later this month.
